                                          PROJECT NO. 58481


    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE §                             PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    LOAD INTERCONNECTION          §                                         OF
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561  §                                       TEXAS


                ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND COMMENTS
______________________________________________________________________________

        Environmental Defense fund (“EDF”) files the following comments in response to the
Commission’s Proposal for Publication (“PFP”) of New 16 TAC §25.194, issued March 12, 2026,
related to the Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §
37.0561 (Project No. 58481), as enacted by Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”).1 The PFP provided that
comments thereon may be filed by April 17, 2026, so these comments are timely filed. Consistent
with the instructions in the PFP, an Executive Summary is appended to these comments.

I.      INTRODUCTION

         EDF appreciates the opportunity to comment on the PFP and commends the Commission
for its efforts to address the myriad challenges posed by large load growth, both in this proceeding
and in the related SB 6 implementation rulemakings. Texas is experiencing an unprecedented surge
in large load interconnection requests, driven largely by data centers, which has significant
implications for system reliability, infrastructure planning, and ratepayer costs. ERCOT projects
that peak demand could reach 218 GW by 2031—up from approximately 86 GW in 2023—
highlighting the scale and pace of anticipated load growth.2 In recognition of this, SB 6 directs the
Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business development while
minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.3
         It is worth emphasizing that traditional approaches to assessing cost causation in
interconnection and transmission planning were developed around incremental, relatively
predictable load growth, under which new delivery facilities were reasonably expected to provide
shared benefits across customer classes over time.4 Modern large load customers represent a

“PFP”, respectively].
2

https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/04/07/8.1-Long-Term-Load-Forecast-Update-2025-2031-and-Methodology-
Changes.pdf.
3
  PURA § 37.0561(a).
4
  Juliet Homer & Jessica Shipley, Proactive Regulatory Approaches to Electrification and Load Growth at iii-iv
(Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Jan. 2025),
https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-37135.pdf

                                                      1
 substantial departure from these assumptions. In many cases, large loads are the primary (and often
exclusive) beneficiaries of upstream transmission upgrades that would historically have been
treated as shared assets. This shift requires a corresponding change in how utilities plan for, incur,
and allocate the costs of new interconnections, in order to ensure alignment between the fees
assessed and the costs each customer group actually imposes on the system.
        As a threshold matter, EDF urges the Commission to center its efforts in this proceeding
around protecting ratepayers from avoidable financial impacts associated with large load
interconnections. The Legislature’s directive under SB 6 reflects the need for delicate policy
balance, one in which economic development goals are best served by a fee structure that
incentivizes investment while protecting customers from unfair cost-shifts. Indeed, a failure to
align interconnection fees with the costs that large loads impose on the system risks undermining,
rather than advancing, long-term economic development by unreasonably shifting costs onto
customers not responsible for them, harming their own economic development capacity. And while
some large load developers may equate incentive to invest in Texas with minimizing their own
upfront costs, that perspective is misaligned with the intent of SB 6 and with the Commission’s
broader obligation to ensure just and reasonable rates for all customers.5
        The Commission should therefore prioritize interconnection rules (including fees) that
ensure large loads pay the incremental costs of new facilities built to serve them, plus a reasonable
share of the embedded costs of the existing transmission system. The Commission is rightly
considering interconnection fees as a tool to discourage speculative interconnection requests, and
EDF generally supports this approach, provided it appropriately reflects all relevant underlying
costs. Properly aligning interconnection standards with cost-causation principles would also send
clearer market signals, create incentives for needed load management, and help mitigate long-term
transmission cost growth.

II.      DISCUSSION

      A. General Fee Structure

        Broadly, the PFP would establish a financial framework for large load interconnections,
beginning with non-refundable tiered study fees of $100,000 for loads between 75 and 250 MW,
and $300,000 for projects exceeding 250 MW.6 At the intermediate agreement stage, customers
must post a partially-refundable financial security of $50,000 per MW (“Refundable
Interconnection Fee”), a requirement that was reduced from $100,000/MW over concern “that the
dollar amount proposed by Staff may unintentionally deter otherwise viable development.” 7 This
reduction also applies to the final non-refundable interconnection fee, which was lowered to
$50,000/MW of contracted peak demand (“Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee”). Furthermore,
under the proposal, large loads are responsible for 100% of direct interconnection costs through

5
  PURA § 11.002(a).
6
  PFP at 13-14.
7
  Id. at 15; Project No. 58481, Commissioner Memorandum at 1 (Mar. 11, 2026).

                                                      2
 nonrefundable Contributions in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”), which cover all facilities built
specifically to connect the customer to the grid (“Direct Connection CIAC”).8 Finally, once
energized, a developer may forfeit up to 80% of its remaining financial security balance for
withdrawing all or a portion of requested peak demand after outstanding interconnection-related
costs are paid.9
         EDF understands that upfront interconnection fees could, in concept, secure large load
customers’ payments of costs they incur. A Refundable Interconnection Fee secures the customer’s
contribution toward embedded system costs, which are reflected in the transmission rates charged
to the customer. A Nonrefundable Interconnection Fee recovers the incremental costs imposed by
the customer that are not included in the customer’s Direct Connection CIAC. Such costs would
include transmission network upgrades triggered by (or otherwise needed to serve) the large load
customer, but which do not directly interconnect the customer to the transmission system. These
costs should properly be allocated to the large load customer, but they will often be challenging to
identify and assess on a customer-by-customer basis, and thus may be appropriate to recover
through a generic per-MW fee grounded in average costs.
         As noted above, EDF supports this conceptual structure. However, the proposed rule’s
initial fee amounts appear to lack a clear cost basis, and there is reason to question whether even
the originally-proposed higher fees fully reflect the incremental and embedded system costs
associated with large load interconnections.10 For example, a recent review of data from PPL
Electric’s Pennsylvania service territory suggests that its incremental transmission upgrade costs
associated with new large load interconnections—not including any share of embedded system
costs—may be closer $164,000 per MW.11 Although this figure is not directly transferable to
ERCOT, it is instructive as a data point from another region experiencing rapid data center–driven
load growth.
         Accordingly, EDF recommends that the Commission establish a transparent process for
periodically reviewing and updating large load interconnection fees. As part of this process, the
Commission should consider conducting a cost-of-service study to quantify the full incremental
and embedded system costs associated with large load interconnections in ERCOT. Such an effort
would be consistent with the Legislature’s direction in SB 6 to evaluate the Four Coincident Peak
(“4CP”) methodology in Project No. 58484, with the goal of ensuring that all loads appropriately
contribute to the recovery of transmission system costs.12 Following completion of a cost-based
evaluation, the Commission should recalibrate the proposed fee structure based on the results of

9

10

MW following Chairman Gleeson’s March 11 Memorandum and subsequent discussion at the PUCT Open Meeting.

   Surrebuttal Testimony of Ron Nelson on behalf of Environmental Intervenors, Pennsylvania Public Utility

12

 that study to ensure that interconnection fees accurately reflect system impacts and prevent unfair
cost shifting to other ratepayers.

     B. CIAC & Tax Treatment

         The Commission should clarify that large load customers’ CIAC payments required under
§ 25.194(f)(9) include associated income tax. CIAC payments are generally treated as taxable
income, which means utilities incur additional income tax liability as a direct result of receiving
those payments. This additional tax liability, if not recovered as part of the customer’s CIAC
payment, is shifted onto other customers.
         The current proposed rule probably includes tax gross-up as part of customers’ CIAC
payments, but may leave room for future confusion. Proposed rule § 25.194(f)(9)(A) provides that
direct interconnection costs subject to CIAC “include all costs associated with facilities built to
interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system . . . .” Although the costs
associated with a large load customer’s CIAC payment necessarily includes the incremental tax
liability, a large load customer might (conceivably) argue that such tax liability is not directly
“associated with the facilities” themselves, and therefore such costs should not be included in their
CIAC responsibility. Moreover, EDF understands that TDUs may already gross-up customer
CIACs for taxes, but this practice is not always clearly reflected in their tariffs.13
         Therefore, for the avoidance of doubt, the Commission should clarify that “all costs
associated with the facilities” comprising a customer’s CIAC obligation includes tax gross-up,
such as through the following revision to § 25.194(f)(9)(A):

         (A) Direct interconnection costs include all costs associated with facilities built to
             interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system, including
             radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large
             load customer¸ and applicable tax gross-ups and franchise fees. CIAC must
             be paid in the form of a direct cash payment.

        The Commission should ensure that large load customers fully fund both the direct
infrastructure costs of their interconnections and the associated downstream impacts, consistent
with fundamental principles of cost-causation and SB 6’s directive to protect ratepayers from
unjustified cost-shifting.14




13
   For example, CenterPoint Houston Electric’s tariff, Chapter 6, subsection 2.3, “Transmission Voltage Facility
Extension,” suggests that customer reimbursements can be subject to tax gross-up, but does not specifically mandate
this practice. In contrast, Oncor’s tariff rule 6.2.1 governing CIAC is more explicit: “To the extent that the payment
[of the CIAC Amount] is considered taxable revenue to the Company, it shall include an amount equal to the
Company’s tax liability. The CIAC Amount shall also include an amount to recover franchise fees where
applicable.”
14
   PURA § 37.0561(a).

                                                          4
      C. Disclosure Requirements

        The proposed rule appropriately requires a large load customer to disclose how it intends
to procure power and whether it will rely on onsite generation that serves the load exclusively and
does not export energy to the ERCOT system, consistent with PURA § 37.0561. These disclosures
represent an important first step toward improving transparency around large load development
and enabling ERCOT and interconnecting utilities to better assess system impacts. However, while
the PFP’s definition appropriately distinguishes behind-the-meter resources from export-capable
generation, EDF urges the Commission to require additional disclosures regarding customers’
backup generation and load behavior to provide a more complete and accurate understanding of
how these resources are actually deployed and relied upon in practice.
        In its recent Order in the large load forecasting docket (Project No. 58480), the
Commission declined to adopt more detailed technical and operational disclosure requirements
proposed by EDF and other stakeholders, concluding that such information was “outside the scope
of that rulemaking” and “more appropriately addressed” in this proceeding.15 Project No. 58481
therefore provides the proper forum to incorporate those disclosures, several of which remain
absent from the current PFP despite their relevance to reliability, planning, and emergency
operations. EDF therefore reiterates and incorporates by reference its relevant recommendations
and explanations contained within Environmental Defense Fund’s Initial Comments on Proposed New
16 TAC §25.370 Relating to ERCOT Large Load Forecasting Criteria, filed October 17, 2025, in Docket
No. 58480. Specifically, in its final regulations adopted here, the Commission should require large
load customers to disclose:

        1. The average amount of energy consumption used during a normal set of circumstances;
        2. Any factors or events that would cause the large load customer or flexible large load
           customer to increase or decrease the energy consumption or demand;
        3. Real or reactive power consumption changes and recovery time;
        4. How long the customer remains connected to the grid during a given voltage and/or
           frequency disturbance;
        5. Grid connection level;
        6. Request for firm or flexible load, and how much;
        7. The name and contact information of at least two individuals with decision-making
           authority for ERCOT to have a direct open line of communication in the event of an
           energy emergency alert or grid disturbance.

       Furthermore the Commission should also clarify and strengthen § 25.194(f)(7), "Power
Supply," to require large load customers to disclose the extent to which, and how, they will "bring

15
  See generally, Project No. 58480, Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting Criteria Under PURA
37.0561, Order Adopting New 16 TAC §25.370 (Feb. 6, 2026) [hereinafter “Project No. 58480”]; See also
Environmental Defense Fund’s Initial Comments on Proposed New 16 TAC §25.370 Relating to ERCOT Large
Load Forecasting Criteria (Oct. 17, 2025).

                                                    5
 their own generation" to the system.16 As drafted, § 25.194(f)(7) provides, “[a] large load customer
must disclose how it plans to procure power and whether the large load customer has on-site
generation that will provide power exclusively to the large load customer.17 While this represents
a useful starting point, this does not necessarily require the customer to identify how much of their
power would come from new generation. Such information would aid resource adequacy
modeling, as it allows ERCOT to distinguish between loads that merely reallocate existing grid
capacity and those that facilitate the entry of incremental generation. EDF therefore recommends
the Commission revise § 25.194(f)(7) accordingly:

        (7) Power supply. A large load customer must disclose how it plans to procure power,
        including the extent to which its anticipated load will be served by on-site, co-located,
        or other customer-specific generation resources, and whether such generation will
        provide power exclusively to the large load customer. Such disclosure shall include an
        estimate of the portion of the customer’s expected load to be served by new generation
        resources, the expected availability of those resources during peak system conditions,
        and any anticipated changes in the customer’s reliance on energy supplied by the
        ERCOT system over time.

        Finally, EDF agrees with Texas Industrial Energy Consumers’ (“TIEC”) recommendations
that applicants be required to disclose whether they intend to be the ultimate end-use customer,
and that ERCOT clearly distinguish how submitted data will be used for transmission planning
versus resource adequacy purposes.18 As TIEC has noted, many interconnection requests are
submitted by third-party developers who intend to transfer or lease projects to future tenants rather
than serve as the end-use customer themselves. Requiring this disclosure would improve
“situational awareness” and increase the accuracy and reliability of large load forecasting
assumptions.19

     D. Energization

    Broadly, EDF agrees with several stakeholder comments regarding energization and
interconnection milestones and supports thoughtful approaches that can accelerate energization,
allow flexible load management, and provide customers with greater certainty without
undermining reliability or exposing ratepayers to undue risk.20


16
   PFP at 13.
17
   Id.
18
   Project No. 58480, Texas Industrial Energy Consumers’ Proposed Comments to Draft Rule 25.504 at 3-4 (Oct. 17,
2025).
19
   Id. at 11.
20
   See, e.g., Project No. 58481, Google and Lancium Joint Comments to Staff Proposed Proposal for Publication at
1-2 (Dec. 18, 2025); See also, Luminary Strategies LLC Speed to Power Concept for ERCOT Large Load Batch
Study Proceedings at 1 (Feb. 26, 2026).

                                                       6
     First, EDF agrees with elements of Luminary’s “speed to power” framework supporting a
streamlined energization process whereby large loads may connect to the grid earlier if they agree
to be flexible and controllable.21 As EDF understands this framework, loads registered as ERCOT
controllable load resources (“CLRs”) would be curtailed before firm load shed (e.g., residential
customers) when local grids are constrained, but would not be treated like emergency firm load
shed. This would allow for provisional energization before major network upgrades are complete,
as the load assumes the risk of being curtailed during grid constraints.22 Where appropriately
deployed, these approaches could enable provisional energization several years earlier than
traditional timelines, with the load assuming the operational risk of curtailment during periods of
grid constraint, similar to “flexible interconnections” being piloted elsewhere.23
        EDF also supports the principle of “topological neutrality,” which would allow projects to
use offsite portfolio resources—such as Energy Storage Resources or generation—to address local
nodal constraints.24 As Luminary notes, this model has been implemented elsewhere, including in
Michigan, where a 1.4 GW data center energy plan was approved which relied on off-site battery
storage and existing infrastructure “funded entirely by the developer in a 1:1 ratio of BESS MWs
to Load MWs (4 hour duration BESS).”25
        EDF further agrees that where the Commission imposes significant upfront financial
obligations on large load customers to ensure projects will materialize, those customers should, in
turn, be afforded a reasonable degree of certainty regarding when interconnection and energization
are likely to occur. Meaningful milestones and indicative timelines help ensure that these
requirements are fair, administrable, and effective. Concepts such as Eolian’s proposed two track
readiness framework—which would distinguish between projects operating under compressed
commercial timelines and those on a traditional path—can help customers make informed
decisions while improving planning outcomes, without committing the utility to premature
investment.26

         EDF also agrees that customers’ energization should “distinguish between customer-driven
delays versus delays caused by . . . circumstances outside their control;”27 however, the mere
existence of a circumstance outside the customer’s control should not necessarily excuse
nonperformance. Certain factors may be outside a customer’s direct control, but still within their
ability to influence or mitigate through prudent planning, procurement, contracting, and risk
management. Site permitting is one such example. It is reasonable (and necessary) for customers
and utilities to be held accountable not only for factors squarely within their control, but also, to a
meaningful extent, for risks they are well-positioned to anticipate and manage. Interconnection
rules should therefore avoid overly broad exemptions for energization timelines that would
undermine their purpose.
        EDF has advanced similar recommendations in other proceedings, supporting milestone
frameworks that balance flexibility with enforceable backstops to protect ratepayers and ensure
sound system planning.28 When properly designed, such an approach can provide large load
customers with reasonable certainty while preserving the Commission’s ability to deter speculative
development and prevent stranded infrastructure risk.

III.    CONCLUSION

       EDF thanks the Commission for its attention to this important matter and for the
opportunity to comment. Consistent with the instructions in the PFP, please see following page for
a standalone Executive Summary.

Date: April 17, 2026

                                                          Respectfully Submitted,

                                                          Casey Horan
                                                          Attorney, Electrification
                                                          Environmental Defense Fund
                                                          (212) 624-8888

(February 19, 2026).
28

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND COMMENTS

  Submitting Entity: Environmental Defense Fund

  Summary of Substantive Recommendations:
    A. General Fee Structure
           i. Retain overall fee structure, but ensure fees are tied to system costs in
              keeping with cost-causation principles.
          ii. Establish a transparent, recurring process for reviewing and updating large
              load interconnection fees, supported by a future cost-of-service or similar
              study.
         iii. Periodically recalibrate fees based on study results to ensure they accurately
              reflect system impacts and prevent unfair cost-shifting.
    B. CIAC & Tax Treatment
           i. Explicitly clarify in rule text that large-load CIAC obligations include
              applicable tax gross-ups and franchise fees, to prevent shifting tax liability
              to other customers.
    C. Disclosure Requirements
           i. Incorporate by reference EDF’s prior disclosure recommendations from the
              large-load forecasting docket (Project No. 58480), which the Commission
              identified as more appropriately addressed here.
          ii. Strengthen “Power Supply” disclosures (§ 25.194(f)(7)) to require large
              loads to disclose how much of anticipated demand will be served by new
              generation, the availability of that generation during peak system
              conditions, and expected changes over time in reliance on grid-supplied
              power.
         iii. Require disclosure of whether the applicant is the ultimate end-use customer
              and clarify how information will be used for transmission planning vs.
              resource adequacy modeling.
    D. Energization Timelines
           i. Allow accelerated and provisional energization of new large loads through
              solutions that enable flexibility, controllability, and the use of off‑site
              resources, so customers can connect earlier without undermining reliability
              or shifting risk to ratepayers.
          ii. Support implementing meaningful energization milestones and indicative
              timelines that provide predictability to developers and utilities.

    B. CMC & Tax Treatment

         The Commission should clarify that large load customers' CIAC payments required under
§ 25.194(f)(9) include associated income tax. CIAC payments are generally treated as taxable
income, which means utilities incur additional income tax liability as a direct result of receiving
those payments. This additional tax liability, if not recovered as part of the customer's CIAC
payment, is shifted onto other customers.
         The current proposed rule probably includes tax gross-up as part of customers' CIAC
payments, but may leave room for future confusion. Proposed rule § 25.194(f)(9)(A) provides that
direct interconnection costs subj ect to CIAC "include all costs associated with facilities built to
interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system                 " Although the costs
associated with a large load customer's CIAC payment necessarily includes the incremental tax
liability, a large load customer might (conceivably) argue that such tax liability is not directly
" associated with the facilities" themselves , and therefore such costs should not be included in their
CIAC responsibility. Moreover, EDF understands that TDUs may already gross-up customer
CIACs for taxes, but this practice is not always clearly reflected in their tariffs.13
         Therefore, for the avoidance of doubt, the Commission should clarify that "all costs
associated with the facilities" comprising a customer's CIAC obligation includes tax gross-up,
such as through the following revision to § 25.194(f)(9)(A):

         (A) Direct interconnection costs include all costs associated with facilities built to
             interconnect the large load customer to the existing ERCOT system, including
               radial lines and substation upgrades necessary to interconnect the new large
               load customer, and applicable tax gross-ups and franchise fees. CIAC must
               be paid in the form of a direct cash payment.

        The Commission should ensure that large load customers fully fund both the direct
infrastructure costs of their interconnections and the associated downstream impacts, consistent
with fundamental principles of cost-causation and SB 6's directive to protect ratepayers from
unjustified cost-shifting.14

     C. Disclosure Requirements

         The proposed rule appropriately requires a large load customer to disclose how it intends
to procure power and whether it will rely on onsite generation that serves the load exclusively and
does not export energy to the ERCOT system, consistent with PURA § 37.0561. These disclosures
represent an important first step toward improving transparency around large load development
and enabling ERCOT and interconnecting utilities to better assess system impacts. However, while
the PFP's definition appropriately distinguishes behind-the-meter resources from export-capable
generation, EDF urges the Commission to require additional disclosures regarding customers'
backup generation and load behavior to provide a more complete and accurate understanding of
how these resources are actually deployed and relied upon in practice.
       In its recent Order in the large load forecasting docket (Project No. 58480), the
Commission declined to adopt more detailed technical and operational disclosure requirements
proposed by EDF and other stakeholders, concluding that such information was "outside the scope
of that rulemaking" and "more appropriately addressed" in this proceeding. 15 Project No. 58481
therefore provides the proper forum to incorporate those disclosures, several of which remain
absent from the current PFP despite their relevance to reliability, planning, and emergency
operations. EDF therefore reiterates and incorporates by reference its relevant recommendations
and explanations contained within Environmental Defense Fund s' Initial Comments on Proposed New

load customers to disclose:

interconnection milestones and supports thoughtful approaches that can accelerate energization,
allow flexible load management, and provide customers with greater certainty without
undermining reliability or exposing ratepayers to undue risk.20

     First, EDF agrees with elements of Luminary's "speed to power" framework supporting a
streamlined energization process whereby large loads may connect to the grid earlier if they agree
to be flexible and controllable.21 As EDF understands this framework, loads registered as ERCOT
controllable load resources ("CLRs") would be curtailed before firm load shed (e.g., residential
customers) when local grids are constrained, but would not be treated like emergency firm load
shed. This would allow for provisional energization before major network upgrades are complete,
as the load assumes the risk of being curtailed during grid constraints.22 Where appropriately
deployed, these approaches could enable provisional energization several years earlier than
traditional timelines, with the load assuming the operational risk of curtailment during periods of
grid constraint, similar to "flexible interconnections" being piloted elsewhere.23
        EDF also supports the principle of"topological neutrality," which would allow projects to
use offsite portfolio resources-such as Energy Storage Resources or generation-to address local
nodal constraints.24 As Luminary notes, this model has been implemented elsewhere, including in
Michigan, where a 1.4 GW data center energy plan was approved which relied on off-site battery
storage and existing infrastructure "funded entirely by the developer in al:1 ratio of BESS MWs
to Load MWs (4 hour duration BESS)."25

         EDF also agrees that customers' energization should "distinguish between customer-driven
delays versus delays caused by... circumstances outside their control;"27 however, the mere
existence of a circumstance outside the customer's control should not necessarily excuse
nonperformance. Certain factors may be outside a customer's direct control, but still within their
ability to influence or mitigate through prudent planning, procurement, contracting, and risk
management. Site permitting is one such example. It is reasonable (and necessary) for customers
and utilities to be held accountable not only for factors squarely within their control, but also, to a
meaningful extent, for risks they are well-positioned to anticipate and manage. Interconnection
rules should therefore avoid overly broad exemptions for energization timelines that would
undermine their purpose.
        EDF has advanced similar recommendations in other proceedings, supporting milestone
frameworks that balance flexibility with enforceable backstops to protect ratepayers and ensure
sound system planning.28 When properly designed, such an approach can provide large load
customers with reasonable certainty while preserving the Commission's ability to deter speculative
development and prevent stranded infrastructure risk.

  Submitting Entity: Environmental Defense Fund

  Summary of Substantive Recommendations:
    A. General Fee Structure
            i. Retain overall fee structure, but ensure fees are tied to system costs in

               load interconnection fees, supported by a future cost-of-service or similar

            i. Explicitly clarify in rule text that large-load CIAC obligations include
               applicable tax gross-ups and franchise fees, to prevent shifting tax liability
               to other customers.
    C. Disclosure Requirements
            i. Incorporate by reference EDF's prior disclosure recommendations from the
               large-load forecasting docket (Project No. 58480), which the Commission
               identified as more appropriately addressed here.
           ii. Strengthen "Power Supply" disclosures (§ 25.194(f)(7)) to require large
               loads to disclose how much of anticipated demand will be served by new
               generation, the availability of that generation during peak system
               conditions, and expected changes over time in reliance on grid-supplied
               power.
          iii. Require disclosure ofwhether the applicant is the ultimate end-use customer
               and clarify how information will be used for transmission planning vs.
               resource adequacy modeling.
    D. Energization Timelines
            i. Allow accelerated and provisional energization of new large loads through
               solutions that enable flexibility, controllability, and the use of off-site
               resources, so customers can connect earlier without undermining reliability
               or shifting risk to ratepayers.
           ii. Support implementing meaningful energization milestones and indicative
               timelines that provide predictability to developers and utilities.
